newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Southern Albania town quiet, tense after funeral.
newsitem.headline: Southern Albania town quiet, tense after funeral.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians staged a noisy anti-government protest in the southern town of Vlore on Tuesday, hours after the emotional funeral of a man killed in street battles with riot police.

More than 10,000 people massed in Independence Square, where protesters last week staged five days of peaceful rallies blaming the government for the collapse of pyramid investment funds before violence first erupted on Sunday evening.

"We have come to Vlore to establish a dialogue between the people and the government, to solve the economic crisis and later the political crisis," Neritan Ceka, leader of the centre-right Democratic Alliance, told the cheering crowd.

The demonstrators dispersed later without any signs of renewed clashes, leaving the town quiet but tense. Security forces kept out of sight, and the police station, scene of the most violent incidents on Monday, appeared abandoned.

In the capital Tirana, 150 km (90 miles) to the north, parliament adjourned a debate on Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's proposal to introduce emergency rule in Vlore after deputies from Vlore urged the chamber to think again.
It was not immediately clear whether parliament would reconvene on Wednesday.

Opposition politicians have accused Berisha's party of using proceeds from the investment funds to finance their re-election campaign last year. Western observers have criticised the election as unfair.
Ceka told Reuters Television it was high time for the international community to take a firm stance on the increasingly violent situation in the small Balkan nation.
"It is time that Europe reacts (and) not leave these people to be killed by the government," he said. "There is a risk that tomorrow the army could come in to organise a massacre."
Tens of thousands of mourners poured through Vlore earlier in the day in an explosion of outrage at the death of a demonstrator killed on Monday.
"The police killed him!" a crowd of at least 30,000 shrieked as it filed behind the open coffin of Artur Rustemi, a shopowner who died of a bullet wound during the street clashes.
Rustemi, 33, was one of three people to die in two days of clashes between police and protesters who blame Berisha for the failed investment funds.

The mid-morning cortege through the streets of the port was led by three men carrying black-and-red national flags at half mast. Also held aloft were two portraits of Rustemi, a Moslem father of two who had invested his savings in the schemes.
"Berisha is filling our cemeteries!" cried the mourners, clapping in unison. The crowd was swelled by thousands of residents persuaded to leave balconies overlooking the route and join the march.
One of Rustemi's four brothers said outside the family home: "The police killed him when he was asking for his money."
As marchers moved towards the harbour and on to a cemetery, the local Democratic Party was engulfed in flames and gutted within minutes. It was not clear what had started the blaze.
The other victim of Monday's street battles, who died of heart failure, was buried later in the day. About 150 people were injured in two days of clashes in the port.
In Tirana, about 150 protesters staged a brief protest in central Skanderbeg Square. About 2,000 people gathered for a second straight day in the southern city of Gjirokaster.
The opposition Forum for Democracy has called another rally in Tirana for Wednesday, but the government has issued a fresh ban on the gathering.
